extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and policymakers concerned with novelty/prior-art assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for when a disclosure counts as prior art for novelty and inventive step/obviousness, including means, timing, place, recipient, evidence burdens, and special issues for new media (internet, encryption, paywalls). Covers multiple jurisdictions (Switzerland/EPC, UK, USA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute novelty requirement (Switzerland/EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures are to be looked at independently from the means, the time, the place and the recipient of the information (i.e. 'absolute' novelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a contracting state of the EPC Switzerland has aligned its law so that standards for disclosures in the state of the art are governed by the Strasbourg Convention and generally referred to as an 'absolute' novelty requirement. The disclosure through new media does not require new substantive rules; the main issue is proof of disclosure in individual cases. Recommendation: create public/state-controlled archives to ease burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of disclosure (UK: Section 2(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art ... shall be taken to comprise all matter (whether a product, a process, information about either, or anything else) which has at any time before the priority date of that invention been made available to the public (whether in the United Kingdom or elsewhere) by written or oral description, by use or in any other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UK practice treats any matter made available to the public anywhere before the priority date as relevant to novelty and inventive step. This is supported by EPO/UK case law (e.g., Milliken, Asahi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of prior art (US: 35 U.S.C. § 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102 identifies printed publications, public use, on-sale, patents, and other categories as disclosures that may constitute prior art for novelty and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: US case law further refines these categories (e.g., printed publication = public accessibility; on-sale bar requires commercial offer + invention ready for patenting per Pfaff v. Wells Electronics). Pending published applications become prior art as of their filing; unpublished applications may be relevant in interference/priority contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is enabling if a skilled person can reproduce its teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both EPO/UK practice and case law treat 'enabling disclosure' as key. Non-enabling or erroneous contemporaneous disclosures may not form part of the state of the art (e.g., T77/87).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality/exceptions to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is disclosed when its disclosure from one party to another is unfettered by confidentiality obligations; information in breach of confidentiality is not disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encryption or mere password-protection does not automatically make information confidential (Mars UK v Teknowledge). Passwords are treated like electronic keys; whether access to the password is restricted is decisive. Fee-based (paid) information accessible to anyone for a charge is generally not confidential. Disclosure at international exhibitions may be subject to statutory exceptions if filings are made within specified grace periods (UK Section 2(4)(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of disclosure: recognised forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognised means include written or oral disclosure, use, and 'in any other way' — i.e. any form of making information available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral disclosure and prior use are recognised but may be harder to prove. Electronic forms (web pages, e-mail) are treated similarly depending on accessibility and protection measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure is generally irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures made available to the public anywhere in the world before the priority date are relevant to novelty/inventive step; the place of disclosure is not decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some theoretical distinctions exist (server location vs. place where disclosure is perceived), practice under EPC/UK/US treats place as irrelevant. National exceptions may apply linked to local contract/employment/confidentiality law (Lux Traffic v Pike Signals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and duration of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The date (day) of disclosure is essential; the durability/duration of availability is not essential — even short availability can be prejudicial to novelty/inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic timestamps may be unreliable; certified archives are desirable for evidentiary certainty. Old publications remain prior art regardless of age unless 'lost art' (evidence no longer available).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standards of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting a prior publication bears the burden of proof that the disclosure occurred and was available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral testimony or interested witnesses generally requires corroboration; EPO may require 'beyond reasonable doubt' for prior use. There should be uniform evidentiary rules across disclosure modes to preserve legal certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet/new media disclosures treated as publications if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on the World-Wide Web is considered published unless the information is protected in some way (e.g., by restricting access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-mail is likened to letter (private) unless publicly posted. Search engines index what is publicly accessible; indexing does not create confidentiality. Potential for manipulation does not in principle require different substantive rules, but raises evidentiary questions and supports the desirability of certified archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient capability and comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral disclosure to an audience that is not in a position to understand the invention does not constitute a prejudicial disclosure to that audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a third party can determine the invention by disassembly or reverse engineering, that constitutes prejudicial disclosure; the relevant disclosure date is when reverse engineering could have taken place (G1/92, T461/88).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private knowledge and secret portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge or private, non-public information (e.g., kept in a portfolio and not communicated) does not constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use must be public or at least accessible to the public; mere absence of affirmative concealment may suffice for 'public use' in some contexts, but secret/private knowledge is not prior art (Alexander Milburn Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar (United States specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that was on sale in the U.S. more than one year prior to the U.S. filing date is barred from patenting (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pfaff v. Wells: two conditions required before the critical date — (1) a commercial offer for sale, and (2) the invention ready for patenting (actual reduction to practice or enabling drawings/descriptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of copending/pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Copending patent applications that are eventually published can be relevant to novelty; unpublished copending applications generally are not relevant (with jurisdictional variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UK: co-pending applications with earlier priority that eventually publish are relevant to novelty; unpublished ones are not. US: pending unpublished US and foreign applications may be used in interference proceedings for priority (35 U.S.C. § 102(g)); once published or issued they are prior art as of their filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use is not regarded as public use for the purpose of defeating patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinally intended to give inventors time to test/verify suitability of the invention (e.g., Lough v. Brunswick Corp.). Courts examine whether use was 'experimental' vs ordinary public use.
